explanation: Split the list with slow/fast pointers, sort both halves recursively, then merge their original nodes. Choosing the left node on equal values preserves the relative order of ties.
spaceComplexity: O(log n) recursion space; nodes are reused.
attribution: Original C# implementation and explanation authored for EPI Practice from the displayed problem contract; EPI problem attribution remains in the collection.
correctness: Splitting decreases the list size, so induction gives two sorted halves. The merge repeatedly selects the least head, preserving sorted order and every original node. On equal values it selects from the left half first. Since all left-half nodes originally preceded right-half nodes, and recursive calls preserve their internal tie order, the complete merge sort is stable.
walkthrough: Label the two 7-valued nodes in [7, 3, 7, 1] as 7a and 7b. The halves sort to [3, 7a] and [1, 7b]. Merging emits 1, then 3; at the tie it takes 7a before 7b. Return values [1, 3, 7, 7], with the original equal-valued nodes still in their original order.
edgeCases: Null and one-node lists are already sorted.
Repeated values must preserve node order, not merely sorted values.
The list is split before recursion and original nodes are relinked rather than copied.
